open_obligations: Note that Burns et al. observed only small bootstrapping improvements on NLP tasks and no improvements in the RM setting in preliminary experiments, so the promising result matched here is from their chess setting
Check Figure 9(b) for the size of the gain and whether it exceeds run-to-run variation
Check which metric the source's 'generalization performance' uses; Burns et al. report performance gap recovered (PGR)
out.other_title: Bootstrapping through intermediate model sizes improves weak-to-strong PGR on chess
out.rationale: This is an explicit 'consistent to the findings in Burns et al.' statement. Burns et al.'s bootstrapping gain was shown in the chess setting and measured as PGR, with only small improvements on NLP tasks and none in the RM setting in preliminary experiments, while this source reports generalization performance (metric not given in the passage) with one intermediate model, so the agreement is in direction only. Both ask whether bootstrapping through intermediate models improves weak-to-strong generalization, but in different settings, and the source's result is not evidence for Burns et al.'s chess result, so the link proposes SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING rather than SUPPORTS.
out.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: Whether bootstrapping through an intermediate model improves weak-to-strong generalization; holds for weak models supervising Mistral-7B; the source's task is harmlessness preference alignment (SimPO on CAI-Harmless) with GPT-2/OPT weak and intermediate models, not Burns et al.'s chess puzzles with GPT-4-family models, so compare with Burns et al.'s preliminary NLP and reward modeling results, where bootstrapping gave only small or no improvements

text: When a weak model supervises Mistral-7B through an intermediate model, the authors find that bootstrapping improves weak-to-strong generalization performance, which they state is consistent with Burns et al. (2024). They add that bootstrapping also lowers their deception score to some extent.
